topic: Ornith 1.5 9B: a frontier-level SWE-bench Verified score out of a four-bit build that fits a mid-range gaming card
title: Ornith 1.5 9B: 70.6 from a 6 GB file
description:
Ornith 1.5 9B and the 6 GB file: a frontier-level score without frontier hardware.

Ornith reports 70.6 on SWE-bench Verified for a 9B dense model whose four-bit GGUF build is 5.63 GB on disk. That is small enough for the mid-range gaming card already in your machine, which is where the "frontier score needs frontier hardware" rule stops holding. The catch: the numbers are Ornith's own, averaged over five runs with the git history stripped and network access disabled.

You'll learn: what the four-bit build actually weighs, what SWE-bench Verified measures, how Ornith ran the evaluation, and the one place the myth still holds.

Model card: https://huggingface.co/ornith-ai/Ornith-1.5-9B-GGUF

Subscribe for more local AI builds. (Narration is AI-generated.)

notes_for_review: Four key numbers spent: the four-bit file size, the SWE-bench Verified score, the five averaged runs, and the parameter count in the payoff. No analogy; the four-bit build gets the plain mechanism instead. SWE-bench Verified is named on screen only, because the acronym has no spoken form in tts_lexicon.json, so the narration says what it measures. top2 and entity_spend fail by design: 'Ornith-1.5' would put an unspoken version number on screen, and the brief forbids spending the GPQA and context-window material.
